title: Matthew 25:31–46
context: Jesus ends the discourse with the Son of Man in glory, angels, and a throne of judgment over all nations. Sheep and goats are separated; the King identifies with ‘the least of these’ in hunger, thirst, strangerhood, nakedness, sickness, and prison. Eternal punishment and eternal life close the chapter—mercy’s fruit revealed, not a rival gospel.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on faith’s fruit, judgment, and love for the needy, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Faith working by love… is the essence… of all true religion… We know that the whole of religion is contained in the love of God and of our neighbour.

I know, the saints who will be placed before the tribunal of the Divine Justice, have had Faith, and through Faith have performed good Works. But… they appear and stand before God with this confidence… that God has set forth his Son Jesus Christ as a propitiation through Faith in his blood… I do not read, that Christ is constituted a propitiation through Works… that we may also be justified by Works.
arminian.source: Works, Vol. 1 (on justification / faith and works)

reformed.quote: Christ does not say that the works are the cause of salvation, but the tokens… by which we may know who are the children of God… God will acknowledge those works as done to himself.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 25:35–40)

reformed.quote: Faith… is the alone instrument of justification; yet… is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but works by love.

verses.text: “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.
verses.arminianNotes:
The meek teacher now sits in open majesty.

The same Jesus who invites also judges. Grace makes the throne good news for those who trust Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Parousia glory and judicial session. Christ alone occupies the glorious throne.

The Judge is the crucified and risen Son. History bends toward His bench.

verses.text: Before him all the nations will be gathered, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.
verses.arminianNotes:
All nations gathered; shepherd-separation of sheep and goats.

The nations truly stand before Him. The gospel’s call matters because this sorting is true.
verses.reformedNotes:
The assembly is universal, and the separation is personal. Shepherd imagery makes the Judge intimate and decisive.

God distinguishes peoples one from another with shepherd certainty.

verses.text: He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.
verses.arminianNotes:
Right and left—honored place versus rejection’s side.

Destination language is not metaphor only. Choose the Shepherd’s voice now.
verses.reformedNotes:
Placement is the King’s act before the sentences are spoken.

Verdict begins in where He sets you.

verses.text: Then the King will tell those on his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;
verses.arminianNotes:
Blessed by the Father, inherit a kingdom prepared from the foundation.

Inheritance language keeps salvation gift, even as works will be cited as evidence. Prepared kingdom means grace older than our charity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Father’s blessing, prepared kingdom, foundation of the world—election’s warmth under inheritance speech.

The kingdom is prepared before our works. Sheep receive what God planned.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear gift in ‘inherit’ and ‘prepared.’ Arminians typically hold preparation together with a history of enabled mercy; Reformed readers press eternal preparation and works as evidences, not purchase price.

verses.text: for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat. I was thirsty and you gave me drink. I was a stranger and you took me in.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hunger, thirst, stranger—met with food, drink, welcome.

Love of neighbor is not optional garnish. Grace that saves creates concrete mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
The King lists embodied cares. Faith’s fruit wears ordinary kindness.

The righteous are known by mercies that mirror the King’s heart.

verses.text: I was naked and you clothed me. I was sick and you visited me. I was in prison and you came to me.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Naked, sick, prison—clothing, visiting, coming near.

Costly presence is kingdom work. Grace pushes toward the overlooked.
verses.reformedNotes:
Visitation and clothing continue the evidence trail.

Holiness is social as well as vertical—love of the least under Christ’s claim.

verses.text: “Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you a drink?
verses.arminianNotes:
The righteous are surprised—they did not keep a scorecard of feeding the King.

True mercy is often unconscious of its greatness. Love is not self-advertising virtue signaling.
verses.reformedNotes:
The surprise of the righteous guards against pride in works. The sheep weren’t trading for a throne.

Evidence can be without being mercenary. God sees what humility forgot to tally.

verses.text: When did we see you as a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you?
verses.arminianNotes:
Stranger and naked likewise unnoticed in their own memory.

Ordinary welcome counts in the King’s ledger of love.
verses.reformedNotes:
The questions continue—unselfconscious righteousness.

The Spirit’s fruit often feels like simply doing the next faithful thing.

verses.text: When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Sick and prison visits also surprise them.

Showing up in hard places is how faith works through love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Presence with the suffering is remembered in heaven even when forgotten on earth.

God wastes no cup of cold water given in the King’s name.

verses.text: “The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Because you did it to the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.

Christ so identifies with His vulnerable people that mercy to them is mercy to Him. Grace teaches us to see Jesus in the least.
verses.reformedNotes:
The King’s ‘Truly’ binds care for His brothers to care for Himself.

Union with Christ makes service to His people service to Him. Works are tokens of belonging, not the root of it.
verses.keyContrast: Christ is served in the least. Arminians typically stress love as the living outworking of a faith that can be resisted or embraced; Reformed interpreters stress Spirit-wrought evidence in the elect without making mercy the meritorious cause of justification.

verses.text: Then he will say also to those on the left hand, ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels;
verses.arminianNotes:
Depart, cursed, eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels.

Arminian interpreters refuse to blunt this: judgment is personal and everlasting. The warning summons repentance and mercy now.
verses.reformedNotes:
The left-hand sentence is as clear as the right-hand blessing. Fire which is prepared for the devil becomes the goats’ place by the King’s word.

Jesus teaches eternal judgment. Holiness and justice meet at this throne.

verses.text: for I was hungry, and you didn’t give me food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink;
verses.arminianNotes:
No food, no drink—omissions named as guilt.

Neglect can damn as surely as open violence. Grace still opens hands while there is time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sins of omission stand in the indictment.

Failing to love is rebellion, not mere incompleteness.

verses.text: I was a stranger, and you didn’t take me in; naked, and you didn’t clothe me; sick, and in prison, and you didn’t visit me.’
verses.arminianNotes:
No welcome, clothing, or visit—absence where presence was owed.

Indifference to the least is indifference to Christ. Turn toward them today.
verses.reformedNotes:
The negative catalog mirrors the sheep’s positives.

What we will not do reveals whom we will not serve.

verses.text: “Then they will also answer, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and didn’t help you?’
verses.arminianNotes:
They too are surprised—claiming they never saw the King in need.

Blindness to the least is self-serving. Ask for eyes grace can give.
verses.reformedNotes:
The goats are surprised too, justifying themselves without fruit.

Empty religion can miss Christ while using His title ‘Lord.’

verses.text: “Then he will answer them, saying, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you didn’t do it to one of the least of these, you didn’t do it to me.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Because you didn’t do it to the least, you didn’t do it to me.

Omission toward the least is omission toward Jesus. The identification cuts both ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
The same Truly binds neglect of the least to neglect of the King.

Christ’s solidarity with His own makes lovelessness personal against Him.

verses.text: These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Eternal punishment and eternal life—parallel forever-words.

Wesleyan Arminians hold both destinies as outcomes meant to move hearers toward Christ and concrete love now.
verses.reformedNotes:
Parallel ‘eternal’ seals the seriousness of both ends.

Jesus teaches everlasting punishment and everlasting life. The Judge’s word stands.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions affirm everlasting outcomes. Arminians typically press the warning as a summons to faith working through love; Calvin’s heirs generally press the certainty of the King’s separation and the evidential role of mercy in those appointed to life.
